name: Strike Lab: Three-Hit Training Arena
request: Create a small, playable Strike Lab fighting-game training arena for one player on desktop and touch. Include a humanoid training dummy, a three-hit light-attack combo with visible windup, contact and recovery animations, synchronized hit sound effects, a visible accepted-hit counter and dummy health. The server must validate attack timing and range. Each accepted strike damages and counts once at contact; swinging out of range, holding the button or spamming during recovery must not create extra hits. Show distinct hit and miss feedback. After defeat, reset the dummy and let the player practice again; provide a clear reset control and an uncluttered arena. Search Marketplace first for complete reusable combat/training components, compatible dummy rigs, existing animations and sound rather than rebuilding everything. Inspect compatibility, behavior and included media, preserve useful working pieces and author only missing integration. Source missing audio from Marketplace and verify actual playing animations and audible sounds. Record an importer capability gap honestly rather than treating it as a bad asset. Choose reasonable styling and damage values yourself. No PvP, matchmaking, saving, monetization or large world. Success needs native evidence for the full combo, exact counting, misses, recovery spam, defeat/reset and desktop/touch controls. A damage script with a static dummy does not meet the animation requirement.

spec.title: Strike Lab: Three-Hit Training Arena
spec.summary:
Strike Lab is a compact one-player fighting-game practice room for desktop and touch. The namespace contains a safe spawn, a focused training mat, a stationary humanoid dummy, restrained boundaries, and a small HUD. At spawn, the player sees the dummy centered across the mat, its health display, an accepted-hit counter, a Light Attack control, and a Reset control. A short approach brings the player into striking range. Mouse button 1 or F on desktop, and a large thumb-reachable touch button on mobile, performs one discrete light-attack input. Three correctly timed presses produce a three-step combo with visible windup, contact, and recovery. The immediate goal is to land all three strikes, see 20, 30, and 50 damage accepted exactly once, defeat the 100-health dummy, observe the KO result, and repeat after reset.

The server owns combo state, contact scheduling, range/front-facing validation, per-swing hit tokens, damage, counters, defeat, and reset. Suggested tuning is 20/30/50 damage; approximately 0.16/0.18/0.24-second windups and 0.24/0.26/0.38-second recoveries; a 0.8-second continuation window after recovery; and a six-stud contact range with a forward-facing check. Exact contact timing should be aligned to verified animation markers when supplied by the retained component. Discrete input may queue only where the audited combo design permits; holding the control never auto-repeats. A miss still shows its full attack motion but produces distinct MISS/whiff presentation, no impact sound, no damage, and no counter increment. Recovery spam is rejected without creating additional attack instances.

An accepted contact flashes or reacts the dummy, emits the verified spatial impact sound once, pulses the hit counter, and updates health. On defeat, the dummy enters a short non-targetable KO state and the HUD briefly preserves the final result before automatic restoration after about 2.5 seconds. Reset is also available at any time through R on desktop and a touch button; it cancels active attack state, restores the dummy to 100 health and its starting transform, clears the current-cycle accepted-hit counter, and returns the combo to step one. The experience deliberately excludes PvP, matchmaking, saving, monetization, progression, and world expansion.

Marketplace behavior and media remain discovery-dependent. No claim of animation, sound, control, or gameplay success is made until native verification records the full combo, exact counting, out-of-range misses, held input, recovery spam, defeat, automatic and manual reset, respawn behavior, and both desktop and touch operation.
spec.visualDirection:
Use a clean near-future sports laboratory rather than a featureless baseplate. The playable footprint is approximately 42 by 32 studs: a charcoal rectangular training mat sits at the center, the dummy occupies a marked target circle near the north end, and the safe spawn faces it from roughly 16 studs away at the south end. Low beveled perimeter rails and solid rear wall panels communicate boundaries without blocking the camera. Leave broad side lanes for circling and range testing, but no unrelated rooms or decorative routes.

Favor simple chamfered panels, horizontal light strips, concentric target markings, and a strong central axis from spawn to dummy. The material hierarchy is matte dark graphite for floor and boundaries, medium cool gray for structure, desaturated cyan for neutral guidance, white for primary text, amber for a miss, vivid red-orange for accepted contact and low health, and green only for ready/reset confirmation. The dummy should remain the brightest physical focal point and have a readable humanoid silhouette against the darker rear wall. Avoid visual clutter, dense props, excessive particles, and lighting that obscures limb motion.

Combat presentation must make phases legible: windup changes the player's silhouette before the hand advances; contact reaches full extension and coincides with accepted feedback; recovery visibly retracts and returns to neutral. Give the three attacks distinct silhouettes and slightly increasing weight. An accepted hit uses a short dummy reaction or displacement-free recoil, red-orange flash/highlight, compact contact burst, counter pulse, health reduction, and one synchronized spatial impact sound. A miss uses amber or gray MISS text and a brief non-impact whiff cue such as an arc or fading reticle, with no red flash and no impact sound. Feedback must not obscure the combatants.

The HUD should occupy restrained screen edges: dummy name and segmented or smoothly updating 100-point health near the top center, accepted hits immediately below, a small three-step combo indicator near the lower center, desktop key hints in one corner, and touch controls in the lower-right safe area. Touch buttons need large targets and clear pressed/disabled states while remaining transparent enough to preserve sight of the mat. Reset should be visually separate from Attack to prevent accidental activation. Scale and safe-area behavior must remain readable across desktop and phone aspect ratios.

playerExperience.title: Strike Lab: Three-Hit Training Arena
playerExperience.summary:
Strike Lab is a compact one-player fighting-game practice room for desktop and touch. The namespace contains a safe spawn, a focused training mat, a stationary humanoid dummy, restrained boundaries, and a small HUD. At spawn, the player sees the dummy centered across the mat, its health display, an accepted-hit counter, a Light Attack control, and a Reset control. A short approach brings the player into striking range. Mouse button 1 or F on desktop, and a large thumb-reachable touch button on mobile, performs one discrete light-attack input. Three correctly timed presses produce a three-step combo with visible windup, contact, and recovery. The immediate goal is to land all three strikes, see 20, 30, and 50 damage accepted exactly once, defeat the 100-health dummy, observe the KO result, and repeat after reset.

The server owns combo state, contact scheduling, range/front-facing validation, per-swing hit tokens, damage, counters, defeat, and reset. Suggested tuning is 20/30/50 damage; approximately 0.16/0.18/0.24-second windups and 0.24/0.26/0.38-second recoveries; a 0.8-second continuation window after recovery; and a six-stud contact range with a forward-facing check. Exact contact timing should be aligned to verified animation markers when supplied by the retained component. Discrete input may queue only where the audited combo design permits; holding the control never auto-repeats. A miss still shows its full attack motion but produces distinct MISS/whiff presentation, no impact sound, no damage, and no counter increment. Recovery spam is rejected without creating additional attack instances.

An accepted contact flashes or reacts the dummy, emits the verified spatial impact sound once, pulses the hit counter, and updates health. On defeat, the dummy enters a short non-targetable KO state and the HUD briefly preserves the final result before automatic restoration after about 2.5 seconds. Reset is also available at any time through R on desktop and a touch button; it cancels active attack state, restores the dummy to 100 health and its starting transform, clears the current-cycle accepted-hit counter, and returns the combo to step one. The experience deliberately excludes PvP, matchmaking, saving, monetization, progression, and world expansion.

Marketplace behavior and media remain discovery-dependent. No claim of animation, sound, control, or gameplay success is made until native verification records the full combo, exact counting, out-of-range misses, held input, recovery spam, defeat, automatic and manual reset, respawn behavior, and both desktop and touch operation.
playerExperience.visualDirection:
Use a clean near-future sports laboratory rather than a featureless baseplate. The playable footprint is approximately 42 by 32 studs: a charcoal rectangular training mat sits at the center, the dummy occupies a marked target circle near the north end, and the safe spawn faces it from roughly 16 studs away at the south end. Low beveled perimeter rails and solid rear wall panels communicate boundaries without blocking the camera. Leave broad side lanes for circling and range testing, but no unrelated rooms or decorative routes.

Favor simple chamfered panels, horizontal light strips, concentric target markings, and a strong central axis from spawn to dummy. The material hierarchy is matte dark graphite for floor and boundaries, medium cool gray for structure, desaturated cyan for neutral guidance, white for primary text, amber for a miss, vivid red-orange for accepted contact and low health, and green only for ready/reset confirmation. The dummy should remain the brightest physical focal point and have a readable humanoid silhouette against the darker rear wall. Avoid visual clutter, dense props, excessive particles, and lighting that obscures limb motion.

Combat presentation must make phases legible: windup changes the player's silhouette before the hand advances; contact reaches full extension and coincides with accepted feedback; recovery visibly retracts and returns to neutral. Give the three attacks distinct silhouettes and slightly increasing weight. An accepted hit uses a short dummy reaction or displacement-free recoil, red-orange flash/highlight, compact contact burst, counter pulse, health reduction, and one synchronized spatial impact sound. A miss uses amber or gray MISS text and a brief non-impact whiff cue such as an arc or fading reticle, with no red flash and no impact sound. Feedback must not obscure the combatants.

The HUD should occupy restrained screen edges: dummy name and segmented or smoothly updating 100-point health near the top center, accepted hits immediately below, a small three-step combo indicator near the lower center, desktop key hints in one corner, and touch controls in the lower-right safe area. Touch buttons need large targets and clear pressed/disabled states while remaining transparent enough to preserve sight of the mat. Reset should be visually separate from Attack to prevent accidental activation. Scale and safe-area behavior must remain readable across desktop and phone aspect ratios.
